newsitem.title: CROATIA: US poll sees Tudjman's party ahead in election.
newsitem.headline: US poll sees Tudjman's party ahead in election.

text.p: A U.S.-sponsored poll gives President Franjo Tudjman's nationalist party a strong lead in Croatian regional elections set for March despite independent local surveys showing an opposition alliance ahead.
The U.S. Information Agency poll, published by a state-run Croatian newspaper on Thursday, predicted the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) would get about 43 percent of votes.
The question asked was: "Which political party do you prefer?" But the Zagreb daily Vjesnik made it sound as if the poll was directly related to the March 16 elections.
USIA, a branch of the State Department, concluded that the HDZ, which ruled Croatia since its 1991 move to independence from federal Yugoslavia, was as strong as ever.

"No other party appears to challenge its position ... No other party receives even half as much support," said the USIA, which did the poll in November. "It appears unlikely that the HDZ will lose its hold on power any time soon."
Moreover, the results showed HDZ popularity substantially rose from an all-time low 28 percent in February 1996.
Of HDZ's main opposition rivals, the Social Liberals (HSLS) would get 19 percent, the Peasant Party (HSS) 18 percent and the formerly communist Social Democrats (SDP) nine percent.
The USIA poll results, obtained in face-to-face interviews with 1,000 adults, contrasted sharply with a survey published in the independent Zagreb weekly Nacional this week.
Nacional surveyed some 3,000 people across the country and said the HDZ won only 28.8 percent of votes, with the HSLS at 25.2 percent, HSS 13.7 and SDP 10.5 percent.

A U.S. embassy spokeswomon said the USIA conducted the poll strictly for its own needs. "The results are not secret but as a rule we don't make them public, nor did we do so on this occasion," she told Reuters.

In a commentary on its survey, USIA said supporters of the three largest parties -- HDZ, HSLS and HSS -- shared "the same nationalist attitudes ... but the intensity of nationalist feelings is substantially stronger among HDZ supporters."
Last month, state media published another USIA survey, also carried out in November.

More than 80 percent of those polled approved of Tudjman's policies. That endorsement inexplicably contradicted what is widely regarded to be serious discontent over corruption-tinged privatisation and Tudjman's authoritarian rule.

Several strikes over wages, working and living conditions shook Croatia in December. In the largest rally some 100,000 people gathered in Zagreb to vent their anger over the government's attempts to shut down independent Radio 101.

Analysts said the 74-year-old Tudjman's unscathed popularity could be partly attributed to popular sympathy for his reported struggle with stomach cancer and the lack of an another charismatic leader.
But diplomats said this week Tudjman was so ill he might have to give up his duties in a matter of months.

Presidential elections are also due in 1997 but analysts say they might not take place at all if HDZ decides to amend the constitution to delay them. The party will still retain a parliamentary majority at least until 1999.
